# Introduction

The plotting module provides a unified suite of visualization functions for environmental monitoring datasets.

All plotting functions support both raw data frames and `env_schema` objects through S3 method dispatch. The system is designed to operate independently of source column names by relying on schema mappings and accessor functions.

Supported visualizations include:

- Time-series plots
- Boxplots
- Correlation plots
- Piper diagrams
- Schoeller diagrams
- Stiff diagrams
- Durov diagrams
- Spatial plots
- Geochemical animations

# Design Philosophy

## Schema-Aware Architecture

All environmental plotting functions ultimately operate on an `env_schema` object.

When a raw data frame is supplied, it is first converted using user-provided column mappings.

For example:

```r
series_plot(
  groundwater_data,
  location = well_id,
  sample_date = sample_date,
  analyte = constituent,
  result = concentration
)
```

internally becomes:

```r
env_schema(
  groundwater_data,
  location = well_id,
  sample_date = sample_date,
  analyte = constituent,
  result = concentration
)
```

Internally, plotting methods interact with schema accessors rather than hard-coded column names:

```r
location_var()
sample_date_var()
analyte_var()
analysis_result_var()
analysis_unit_var()
reporting_flag_var()
```

This architecture ensures plots remain portable across different environmental datasets.

# Example Datasets

The package includes groundwater monitoring datasets that can be used to demonstrate plotting functionality.

## Standardized Example Dataset

The `gw` dataset is an `env_schema` object and can be used directly with plotting functions.

```{r data-gw}
library(dplyr)
library(manager)

data(gw)

gw
```

Because `gw` is already an `env_schema`, no additional mapping is required.

```{r gw-series}
plots <- series_plot(gw)

plots[[1]]
```

## Raw Groundwater Dataset

The `gw_data` dataset contains environmental monitoring data in tabular format.

```{r data-gw-data}
data(gw_data)

glimpse(gw_data)
```

Create a smaller subset for examples.

```{r subset-data}
example_wells <- c(
  "MW-1",
  "MW-2",
  "MW-3"
)

gw_subset <- gw_data %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    location_id %in% example_wells
  )
```

## Creating an env_schema Object

Raw datasets can be converted into an `env_schema` object.

```{r env-schema}
gw_schema <- env_schema(
  gw_subset,
  location = location_id,
  sample_date = sample_date,
  analyte = param_name,
  result = analysis_result,
  unit = default_unit,
  reporting_flag = lt_measure
)

gw_schema
```

# Time Series Plots

## Basic Example

```{r series-basic}
plots <- series_plot(gw)

plots[[1]]
```

## Linear Trend

```{r series-lm}
plots <- series_plot(
  gw,
  trend = "lm"
)

plots[[1]]
```

## Mann-Kendall Trend

```{r series-mk, eval=FALSE}
plots <- series_plot(
  gw,
  trend = "mann_kendall",
  trend_label = "compact"
)

plots[[1]]
```

## Combined Plot

```{r series-combined}
series_plot(
  gw,
  plot_type = "combined"
)
```

## Standards Overlay

```{r series-standards}
plots <- series_plot(
  gw,
  standards = TRUE
)

plots[[1]]
```

# Boxplots

## Basic Boxplot

```{r boxplot-basic}
plots <- boxplot(gw)

plots[[1]]
```

## Display Individual Observations

```{r boxplot-points}

  gw,
  show_points = TRUE
)

plots[[1]]
```

## Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

```{r boxplot-ci}

  gw,
  show_points = TRUE,
  plot_ci = TRUE
)

plots[[1]]
```

## Standards Overlay

```{r boxplot-standards}
plots <- boxplot(
  gw,
  standards = TRUE
)

plots[[1]]
```

## Add Explanation Panel

```{r boxplot-explanation}
plots <- boxplot(
  gw,
  add_explanation = TRUE
)

plots[[1]]
```

# Correlation Plots

Correlation plots require the optional `GGally` package.

```{r corr-plot, eval=FALSE}
corr_plot(
  gw_data,
  constituents = c(
    "Iron, dissolved",
    "Manganese, dissolved",
    "Sulfate, total"
  ),
  sample_locations = c(
    "MW-1",
    "MW-2"
  )
)
```

# Piper Diagrams

## Basic Piper Diagram

```{r piper-basic}
piper_plot(gw)
```

## Normalized Analyte Matching

```{r piper-normalized}
piper_plot(
  gw,
  analyte_matching = "normalized"
)
```

## Exact Analyte Matching

```{r piper-exact}
piper_plot(
  gw,
  analyte_matching = "exact"
)
```

## Scale Point Size by TDS

```{r piper-tds, eval=FALSE}
piper_plot(
  gw,
  scale_analyte = "Total Dissolved Solids"
)
```

## Group by Category

```{r piper-group, eval=FALSE}

  gw,
  group_col = "aquifer_unit"
)
```

# Piper Animations

Create an interactive animation:

```{r piper-animation, eval=FALSE}

```

Export animation:

```{r piper-html, eval=FALSE}

```

plots[[1]]

# Animation Framework

The package includes shared animation helpers for geochemical plotting.

Animated workflows:

- `piper_time_plot()`
- `piper_time_html()`
- `stiff_time_plot()`
- `stiff_time_html()`

All animation utilities automatically determine the mapped date field from the schema metadata.

# Extending the Plotting Framework

New visualization functions should follow the same S3 design pattern used throughout the package.

## data.frame Method

```{r extension-dataframe, eval=FALSE}
my_plot.data.frame <- function(
  df,
  location,
  sample_date,
  analyte,
  result,
  ...
) {

  df <- env_schema(
    df,
    location = {{ location }},
    sample_date = {{ sample_date }},
    analyte = {{ analyte }},
    result = {{ result }}
  )

  my_plot(df, ...)
}
```

## env_schema Method

```{r extension-schema, eval=FALSE}
my_plot.env_schema <- function(
  df,
  ...
) {

  location_col <- location_var(df)

  sample_date_col <- sample_date_var(df)

  analyte_col <- analyte_var(df)

  result_col <- result_var(df)

  ...
}
```

Following this pattern ensures all future visualizations remain independent of source column names while remaining fully compatible with the package schema system.

# Summary

The environmental plotting framework provides:

- Schema-aware plotting
- Support for raw data frames and `env_schema` objects
- Consistent handling of analytical metadata
- Hydrochemical interpretation tools
- Animation support
- Extensible S3-based architecture

By leveraging schema accessors rather than hard-coded field names, plots remain portable, reusable, and robust across diverse environmental datasets.
